collection.title: Woven in Odisha
collection.lead: A pattern planned in yarn. A poem woven into silk. A colour drawn from roots. Follow Odisha’s textile stories into the materials, places and people behind the cloth.
collection.intro: Cloth is a good reason to slow down. Begin with something that catches your eye, learn how it came into being, and carry a better question to the person who made it. These stories open different doors into Odisha’s weaving traditions.

questions.heading: Meet the people behind the cloth
questions.text: Ask who tied, dyed and wove this piece, where the work happened, and how the maker would like to be credited. Arrange a visit and any demonstration fee before travelling; ask before photographing people, homes or designs.

questions.heading: Understand the material
questions.text: Ask about fibre, yarn, dyes and any finishing. Request evidence for a certification claim and keep the maker or seller’s details with the receipt. A photograph, a place name or the word natural cannot certify a particular product.

questions.heading: Let the cloth live well
questions.text: Ask for care instructions specific to this piece: washing or cleaning, drying, storage and whether colours may transfer. Agree the price, measurements, lead time, delivery and return terms before ordering.

collection.limits: A selected introduction, not a complete survey. Workshop access, current sellers, stock, prices and certifications have not been verified. The textile starter spans different regions and is not a checked day route.

cards.title: Sambalpuri Bandha · before the cloth
cards.text: A peacock opens its tail across the cloth. Follow the pattern backwards, and you arrive at a bundle of yarn—and the decisions made before weaving began.

cards.title: Khandua · when a poem becomes cloth
cards.text: A page can be made of thread. In this Khandua, lettering moves across red cloth—an invitation to meet poetry, devotion and the people who weave them together.

cards.title: Kotpad · a colour with roots
cards.text: Before a colour reaches the loom, there is another story to tell. In Kotpad, following the red leads towards roots, dyeing knowledge and the people who keep it alive.

cards.title: Tasar · the silk before the sari
cards.text: Before the border and the drape, there is a cocoon. Follow Tasar from branch to yarn, then towards the places and people who give the silk its next life.

paragraphs.text: NID’s Sambalpur account shows the design taking shape before weaving. Yarn is marked with a handmade measuring scale, then tied where colour must be kept out. To add another colour, already coloured sections are bound and selected sections opened for the next dye bath. The prepared threads are woven into the intended design. This account describes cotton and bought synthetic dyes; it does not establish the fibre or dyes of every Bandha textile.

With that sequence in mind, compare the motif in the pallu photograph with the work visible at the loom. What would you ask the maker about keeping the coloured sections in position? The two photographs are separate records, not stages of one documented commission. The loom photograph does not name its weaver; a textile or surname alone cannot supply a community identity.

related.title: Khandua · when a poem becomes cloth

paragraphs.text: Look first at the lettering in Prateek Pattanaik’s photograph. Its record identifies a Gita Govinda Khandua, but does not name the weaver. The passage has not been transcribed here; the photograph cannot establish a particular commission.

In Diana Sahu’s June 2024 report, Rautapada weaver Gopinath Chandra Das describes seven colours of Khandua for Jagannath’s weekly clothing, sharing a kumbha design. He and Gobinda Das had begun using Karuna Silk for Geeta Govinda Khandua; natural dyes were still a plan. This is a named temple commission, not a description of every retail saree.

For a particular cloth, ask who specified its design, which words it carries, and how its maker explains the intended use. The photographed textile is not identified as the work discussed in Sahu’s report.

related.title: Tasar: the silk before the sari

paragraphs.text: Sudha describes treating yarn with castor oil, cow dung and ash water before repeated aul-bark dyeing, washing and sun-drying to reach the desired shade.
Devyani Prakash describes Kotpad designs inspired by Nasreen Mahemmedi’s abstract lines. Mishra reports these practitioners’ approaches, not universal instructions.

pages.title: Tasar · the silk before the sari
pages.lead: Before the border and the drape, there is a cocoon. Follow Tasar from branch to yarn, then towards the places and people who give the silk its next life.

paragraphs.text: Look at the loops of yarn in the museum photograph. With no painted scene or elaborate border to follow, the material itself takes centre stage: the loose strands, the hanging weight, the light caught along a thread.

This is a museum display, not a working workshop. The photographed display is labelled Tasar Charkha Yarn. It was recorded at the Odisha Crafts Museum in 2018. It gives us a place to begin looking, without pretending to show today’s production or identify a particular weaver.

sections.title: The story has leaves in it

paragraphs.text: The Central Silk Board’s Keonjhar reference lists Arjun and Asan as Tasar host plants, occurring in forests and raised plantations. A silk story can therefore begin with the plants and people supporting the silkworm, well before the loom.

Durga Soren’s photograph brings that earlier world close: fine strands cross a branch beside a cocoon. The photographer identifies the scene as Tasar at Chandua in Odisha; we have not independently identified the species or host tree in the image.

sections.title: A cocoon is not yet a cloth

paragraphs.text: The Central Silk Board’s technical account separates cocoon processing, reeling, spinning and preparation for weaving. Making usable yarn is work in its own right; weaving is another stage. Different tools and yarn types need not follow one identical sequence.

Beside the museum’s basket of cocoons, imagine tracing one strand forward. If you meet someone working with Tasar, ask which stage they know best. Can they show the difference between the cocoon, the prepared yarn and the finished fabric? The most revealing object may be the unfinished one.

sections.title: Put the right Gopalpur on your map

paragraphs.text: Odisha’s handloom department lists Mayurbhanj, Gopalpur, Fakirpur and Mankidia for Tassar sarees and furnishing textiles. Its cluster table places Rasulpur (Gopalpur) in Jajpur district. That is the Gopalpur weaving connection here, distinct from Gopalpur-on-Sea in Ganjam.

Treat these as research leads, not open-door workshop listings. A weaving place does not prove where a particular cocoon was raised or its yarn processed. Confirm the village, host, address and activity directly before travelling; the locations do not form a checked day route.

sections.title: Learn a name behind each stage

paragraphs.text: Begin with the person in front of you: what do they make, and what do they receive from someone else? Ask where the yarn comes from, who prepared it, and what choices shape this fabric. Record names and stories only with permission.

Tasar identifies a silk material; it does not by itself tell you the weave, blend, dye, finishing or treatment of the cocoons. If those details matter to you, ask for evidence for this particular piece. A natural-looking colour is not a certificate, and Tasar alone does not establish an ahimsa or cruelty-free process.

sections.title: Choose something you will live with

paragraphs.text: If handling a sample is welcome, look at how it falls and how the surface changes in the light. Think about how you will actually use it, then ask whether this fibre, weight and construction suit that use.

Ask for the fibre composition, any blend, the maker’s preferred credit and a receipt. Request care advice for the actual dyes and finish: cleaning, drying, storage and possible colour transfer. Agree measurements, price, lead time and return terms before commissioning a piece.
